sections.title: Classification and presentation: the nephrotic–nephritic spectrum

blocks.text: **Nephrotic syndrome** = proteinuria **> 3.5 g/24 h** + **hypoalbuminaemia** + **oedema**. Avid renal sodium retention starts early and is always present, while blood volume can be low, normal or high. **Nephritic syndrome** = **haematuria** with hypertension, oliguria, fluid retention and a reduced or falling GFR. When the whole nephritic picture is present, think **rapidly progressive GN (RPGN)** and investigate urgently.

blocks.title: Nephrotic vs nephritic at a glance
rows: Podocyte injury → leaky filter, little inflammation
Inflammation and cell proliferation, GBM breaks, crescents
Heavy proteinuria (> 3.5 g/day), bland sediment, fatty casts/lipiduria
Haematuria with red cell casts and dysmorphic RBCs; proteinuria usually modest (< 2 g/day)
Oedema (ankles, genitals, abdominal wall; face on waking), frothy urine
Hypertension, oliguria, oedema (periorbital, leg, sacral), cola-coloured urine

blocks.text: The two syndromes are the **ends of one spectrum**, not separate boxes: a nephritic patient can still leak nephrotic-range protein. Think by compartment: disease on the **urinary (podocyte) side** of the filter tends to be nephrotic; disease of the **endothelium/mesangium** tends to be nephritic with haematuria, protein and hypertension.

blocks.title: Grouping by typical presentation
rows: Minimal change, FSGS, membranous nephropathy (+ diabetic nephropathy, amyloid)
Mild nephritic (haematuria, modest protein, slow course)
IgA nephropathy, mesangiocapillary GN (MCGN); Alport's mimics this
Focal necrotising GN (ANCA vasculitis), diffuse proliferative/post-infectious GN, anti-GBM disease; also SLE

blocks.title: Four glomerular syndromes to recognise
items: **Nephrotic syndrome**
**Acute nephritic syndrome**
**Rapidly progressive GN**: renal failure developing over weeks, often with crescents
**Asymptomatic haematuria and/or proteinuria** found on screening (the commonest way glomerular disease is found)

blocks.text: Strictly, **glomerulonephritis** means biopsy-proven inflammation; non-inflammatory disease (e.g. minimal change) is a **glomerulopathy**, though 'GN' is often used loosely for both. **Nephrotic-range proteinuria always points to the glomerulus**: tubular disease does not cause nephrotic syndrome.

Oedema with low albumin: in nephrotic syndrome the **JVP is normal or low** (unless oliguric renal failure). A **raised JVP** suggests heart failure; stigmata of chronic liver disease suggest cirrhosis.

Cut-offs differ between books. Davidson: proteinuria **> 3.5 g/24 h**. Zero to Finals uses > 3 g/24 h and albumin < 25 g/L; Kumar & Clark Essentials uses albumin < 30 g/L. Use Davidson's figure in the exam.

blocks.note: Look at: the spectrum from podocyte diseases (proteinuria) to inflammatory, crescentic diseases (haematuria).

sections.title: Nephrotic-pattern diseases: minimal change, FSGS and membranous

blocks.title: The three classic podocytopathies
rows: Most nephrotic children (≈90%, boys < 5); about 1/4 of adults
Any age; especially people of West African descent (APOL1 variant)
Middle-aged/older adults, mostly men; commonest adult nephrotic cause in Caucasians
Atopy, NSAIDs, lithium, some antibiotics, haematological malignancy
Secondary: HIV, heroin, morbid obesity, chronic hypertension, scarring after earlier injury
Anti-PLA2R autoantibody; secondary: drugs, hepatitis B/C, SLE, malignancy, heavy metals
Abrupt, often severe; proteinuria highly selective
Primary: abrupt, severe, with haematuria/HTN; secondary: more modest
Indolent; may have microscopic haematuria or HTN
Normal LM; EM foot-process fusion; IF negative
Segmental scars in some glomeruli; C3/IgM trapped in scars
Thick GBM, silver-stain 'spikes', granular subepithelial IgG (IgG4) + C3
Supportive for all; immunosuppression for severe or progressive disease
Remits; does not usually progress to CKD
Often steroid-resistant; about 50% ESKD in 10 years; recurs after transplant
Rule of thirds: remit / stay nephrotic / progressive CKD

blocks.text: **Minimal change disease** is reversible podocyte dysfunction, probably due to a circulating factor. Its proteinuria is **'highly selective'**: albumin leaks but immunoglobulins are kept back. In children, oedema may be mostly facial. It is associated with **Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma**, reflecting T-cell dysfunction.

blocks.title: Secondary membranous nephropathy: causes to list
items: **Drugs:** penicillamine, gold, NSAIDs, captopril, probenecid; heavy metals (mercury)
**Infection:** hepatitis B and C, syphilis, schistosomiasis, _P. malariae_
**Autoimmune:** SLE (membranous lupus), thyroiditis
**Malignancy:** lung, colon, stomach and breast carcinoma; lymphoma

blocks.title: FSGS: primary vs secondary
items: **Primary:** abrupt severe nephrotic syndrome; may need up to 6 months of steroids before calling it resistant

**Secondary** (final common path after nephron loss through hyperfiltration): reduced nephron mass, obesity, hypertension, viruses (HIV, parvovirus B19), drugs (heroin, lithium, interferons, calcineurin inhibitors)
Variants: classic, **tip** (best steroid response), **collapsing** (HIV-associated nephropathy, young black patients), perihilar (often secondary), cellular
Secondary FSGS gives heavy proteinuria but rarely full nephrotic syndrome

blocks.text: Membranous nephropathy is autoimmune against a podocyte antigen, usually the **M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R)**: about 75% of idiopathic cases have IgG4 anti-PLA2R antibodies. **Anti-THSD7A** (≈10% of PLA2R-negative cases) should prompt a search for **cancer**.

'Commonest cause of adult nephrotic syndrome' varies by source: Davidson says **membranous** (in Caucasian adults), Step-Up says membranous in non-diabetic adults, and Zero to Finals says FSGS. Answer **membranous** unless the stem stresses West African ancestry (FSGS).
FSGS is **focal**: a biopsy with only a few glomeruli may miss the scars and be read as minimal change. Suspect FSGS when 'minimal change' fails to respond to steroids.

blocks.note: Look at: the five FSGS variants, with sclerotic segments marked (collapsing = HIV pattern).

sections.title: Nephritic-pattern diseases: IgA, post-infectious GN and RPGN

blocks.text: **IgA nephropathy** is one of the commonest GNs and the commonest cause of glomerular haematuria. Non-visible haematuria is almost universal and hypertension is common. Young adults get self-limiting attacks of **visible haematuria within a few days (or less) of an upper respiratory infection**. Biopsy shows **mesangial IgA (and C3)**, and serum IgA is raised in up to half. It is associated with liver disease and coeliac disease. Treatment is mainly **BP control with RAS inhibitors** when there is proteinuria; Davidson notes some evidence for steroids in high-risk patients.

blocks.title: Henoch–Schönlein purpura (systemic IgA vasculitis, mostly children)
items: Petechial/purpuric rash over the **buttocks and lower legs**
**Abdominal pain** from gut vasculitis
**Arthralgia**
**Haematuria** ± proteinuria; biopsy looks like IgA nephropathy
Usually resolves but often relapses; adults and those with heavy proteinuria may progress

blocks.text: **Post-streptococcal GN (PSGN)** follows a group A β-haemolytic streptococcal **throat** infection (about 10 days later) or **skin** infection (longer), mainly in children and young adults. It is immune-complex mediated (diffuse proliferative GN), complement is consumed (**low C3**), and ASO titre is positive in up to 95% after throat infection. Treatment is **supportive**: BP control, salt restriction, diuretics, dialysis if needed. Antibiotics are rarely needed because the infection is over. Prognosis is good, though CKD can appear 20–30 years later. By contrast, GN **during** an infection (staphylococcal infection, endocarditis), more common in older adults, needs antibiotics.

Timing trap: **IgA = haematuria within days** of a URTI (normal C3); **PSGN = weeks later** (low C3). Latency for PSGN varies by book (Davidson ≈10 days after throat infection; others 1–3 weeks, 10–14 days or 2–6 weeks), but it is always weeks, not days.

blocks.title: Rapidly progressive GN: three immunological groups
rows: Post-infectious GN, SLE, HSP/IgA, cryoglobulinaemia, MCGN
Steroids + IV cyclophosphamide or rituximab; maintain with azathioprine or rituximab

blocks.title: Anti-GBM disease
items: Autoantibodies to the **α3 chain of type IV collagen** (found in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes); linked to HLA-DR15
**Goodpasture's disease** = kidney + lung haemorrhage, more common in the young; the elderly often have renal-limited disease
Presents as RPGN with haemoptysis, cough and breathlessness; lung features may come first
Renal function rarely recovers once dialysis-dependent or oliguric at presentation, so diagnose early
GN with lung haemorrhage can also be due to GPA or lupus

blocks.text: **Drug-induced ANCA vasculitis** (usually high-titre MPO-ANCA): propylthiouracil, hydralazine, minocycline, penicillamine. PR3-ANCA is positive in > 90% of active GPA. In the PEXIVAS trial, plasma exchange did **not** reduce deaths or ESKD in ANCA vasculitis.

**Alport syndrome** (usually X-linked type IV collagen defect): haematuria, proteinuria, progressive renal failure and high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Check with genetic testing and a hearing test. Native Alport kidneys never get anti-GBM disease, but a transplant can trigger anti-GBM alloantibodies.

blocks.note: Look at: crescents of macrophages and epithelial cells filling Bowman's space in RPGN.

blocks.title: Quantifying proteinuria on a spot sample (Davidson)
rows: Nephrotic range (≈ > 3.5 g/24 h); almost always glomerular

blocks.title: Urine
items: Dipstick turns positive above about **0.5 g/24 h**; quantify with a **spot PCR** (more reliable than a 24-hour collection)
**> 1 g/day (PCR > 100 mg/mmol)**: glomerular disease likely and a reason to consider biopsy
**Red cell casts** are pathognomonic of GN; dysmorphic RBCs also mean glomerular bleeding ('active sediment'); white cell casts suggest pyelonephritis
Test an **early-morning sample** to exclude **orthostatic proteinuria**: < 1 g/day, only when upright, benign
Lipiduria ('Maltese crosses') may be seen in nephrotic syndrome

blocks.title: Blood tests by suspected cause
rows: Hepatitis B/C and HIV serology, ANA, dsDNA (anti-PLA2R)
Immunoglobulins, protein electrophoresis, Bence Jones protein, serum free light chains

blocks.title: Renal biopsy
items: **Indications:** unexplained AKI/CKD; adult nephrotic syndrome or glomerular proteinuria; atypical or steroid-unresponsive nephrotic syndrome in a child; nephritic syndrome; transplant dysfunction
**Usually not needed:** typical childhood nephrotic syndrome (minimal change: treat first), diabetic nephrotic patients with a typical course, clear-cut PSGN
**Contraindications:** coagulopathy or low platelets, uncontrolled hypertension, kidneys < 60% of predicted size, solitary native kidney (relative)

blocks.title: Biopsy hallmarks
rows: Non-specific trapping of deposits in the scars
Granular IgG (IgG4), PLA2R, C3 along capillary walls; subepithelial deposits
Mesangial proliferation, thick capillary walls, 'tramline' GBM
Subendothelial deposits (immunoglobulin type) or intramembranous dense deposits (complement type)
'Full house': IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C4, C1q
Congo red: apple-green birefringence under polarised light

blocks.title: Histology vocabulary (Davidson)
items: **Focal** = some glomeruli; **diffuse** = > 50% of glomeruli
**Segmental** = part of a glomerulus; **global** = the whole glomerulus
**Necrotising** = area of necrosis, usually vasculitis; **crescentic** = crescent of inflammatory cells in Bowman's space after severe injury
EM: **subendothelial** deposits → nephritic; **subepithelial** → nephrotic (incl. membranous lupus); **intramembranous** → dense deposit disease

blocks.text: 'Diffuse' is defined as > 50% of glomeruli in Davidson but > 75% in Kumar & Clark Essentials. Use Davidson's definition.

Histology narrows the list but rarely clinches one disease: one disease (e.g. lupus) can show several patterns. Amyloid kidneys are often **large** on imaging, and rectal, gum or fat-pad tissue can be sampled instead of the kidney.

blocks.note: Look at: LM panels (normal, FSGS, necrotising, membranous, crescentic) and IF panels (granular IgG, mesangial IgA, linear anti-GBM).
Compare: granular 'lumpy-bumpy' IF of post-infectious GN with linear IF of Goodpasture syndrome.

sections.title: Management and complications of nephrotic syndrome

blocks.title: Consequences of nephrotic syndrome
rows: Low oncotic pressure + avid renal Na retention (secondary hyperaldosteronism)
Ankle, genital, abdominal oedema; ascites, effusions
Urinary loss of antithrombin III, protein C and S; more hepatic procoagulants; platelet aggregation
Consider prophylaxis in severe/chronic cases; avoid bed rest

blocks.title: Supportive care (all causes)
items: **Salt restriction + loop diuretic**; resistant oedema needs combinations (loop + thiazide + amiloride, monitor potassium)
Gut-wall oedema can block oral diuretic absorption, so **IV diuretics** may be needed; salt-poor albumin may help hypovolaemic patients
**ACE inhibitor or ARB** lowers glomerular capillary pressure and so reduces proteinuria
**Normal protein intake**: a high-protein diet worsens proteinuria
Anticoagulate after thrombosis; renal vein thrombosis needs long-term anticoagulation

blocks.title: Disease-specific treatment
rows: Prednisolone (Davidson 1 mg/kg for 6 weeks; Essentials 60 mg/m²/day for 4–6 weeks, then taper). Frequent relapses or steroid-unresponsive: cyclophosphamide or ciclosporin
Prednisolone 0.5–2 mg/kg/day (response slower and less complete than minimal change); ciclosporin, cyclophosphamide or MMF of uncertain benefit
ACEi, diuretics, statin ± anticoagulation for all; rituximab, alkylating agent + steroid, or CNI for severe/progressive disease
BP control, RAS blockade if proteinuric
Supportive: salt/fluid restriction, diuretics, antihypertensives, dialysis if needed
Steroids + IV cyclophosphamide or rituximab; maintain with azathioprine or rituximab
Treat the cause or stop the offending drug (e.g. antiretrovirals + ACEi for HIV nephropathy)

blocks.text: Membranous treatment differs by book. Davidson: high-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide help but are toxic, so keep them for severe nephrosis or falling function. Kumar: **oral steroids alone do not work**; rituximab, alkylating regimens or CNIs induce remission.

AKI in a nephrotic patient is **rarely** due to the glomerular disease progressing. Think **hypovolaemia from over-diuresis** or **renal vein thrombosis** (loin pain, haematuria, falling function; look on ultrasound).

blocks.title: Prognosis
items: **Poor prognostic signs (all GN):** male sex, hypertension, persistent heavy proteinuria, raised creatinine at presentation, rapid decline, tubulo-interstitial fibrosis on biopsy
Sepsis (especially pneumococcal) is a major cause of death in nephrotic patients; thromboembolism is especially common in membranous
PSGN: usually recovers; IgA: about 25% get renal insufficiency; MPGN: about half reach renal failure

blocks.title: Causes of GN with low serum complement (Davidson)
items: **Post-infectious GN**
**Subacute bacterial infection**, especially **endocarditis** (and shunt nephritis)
**SLE**
**Cryoglobulinaemia**
**Mesangiocapillary GN**, usually the complement type

blocks.title: Clues for each low-complement GN
rows: Low C3 (Davidson: C3 and C4 consumed)
Weeks after strep throat/skin infection; raised ASOT
GN during an active infection, older adult; needs antibiotics
Low C3, C4 and especially C1q
Hepatitis C, palpable purpura, arthralgia; MCGN-like biopsy; type II (monoclonal IgM with rheumatoid factor activity)
Chronic infection, HCV; subendothelial deposits, tramline GBM
MCGN, complement type / dense deposit disease
C3 nephritic factor, factor H defects, partial lipodystrophy; intramembranous C3-only deposits

blocks.text: **MCGN (membranoproliferative GN)** is a biopsy pattern, not a single disease: more mesangial cells plus thick capillary walls, presenting with haematuria and proteinuria (nephritic or nephrotic). Davidson splits it into an **immunoglobulin type** (chronic infection, autoimmunity, monoclonal gammopathy; treat the cause ± MMF or cyclophosphamide) and a **complement type** (inherited/acquired complement dysregulation, including dense deposit disease; eculizumab shows promise). Kumar uses EM types 1–3. Prognosis is often poor.

Nephritic picture + **low C3**: think **post-infectious GN, MPGN (incl. mixed cryoglobulinaemia) and lupus**. With a **normal C3**, look elsewhere: **IgA nephropathy** is the classic example (haematuria at the time of the infection), and anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis do not appear on Davidson's low-complement list.

GN with a **visceral (mainly lung) abscess** looks like post-infectious GN, but **complement is normal** and the biopsy shows **no immune deposits**. Antibiotics and drainage restore function in about half.

blocks.note: Look at: type 1 MCGN with subendothelial deposits and tramline GBM vs type 2 with dense intramembranous material.
Use: chart sorting nephritic syndromes by low vs normal serum complement.

cards.front: Three defining features of nephrotic syndrome (Davidson)?
cards.back: Proteinuria **> 3.5 g/24 h**, **hypoalbuminaemia** and **oedema** (with early renal Na retention; hyperlipidaemia is usual)
**Haematuria** (red cell casts) + hypertension + oliguria + fluid retention + reduced/falling GFR; all together suggests RPGN

cards.front: Minimal change disease: light microscopy and EM findings?
cards.back: **Normal** glomeruli on LM; **podocyte foot-process fusion** on EM; IF negative

cards.front: Main target antigen in idiopathic membranous nephropathy?
cards.back: **M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R)** on podocytes (IgG4 antibodies in ≈75%)

cards.front: Outcome of idiopathic membranous nephropathy ('rule of thirds')?
cards.back: About 1/3 remit spontaneously, 1/3 stay nephrotic, 1/3 get progressive CKD

cards.front: Which gene variant explains the high rate of FSGS in people of West African descent?
Haematuria after a URTI: how does timing separate IgA nephropathy from PSGN?
cards.back: IgA: within **a few days** (normal C3). PSGN: about **10 days** after throat infection, longer after skin infection (low C3)
Purpuric rash on buttocks/legs, abdominal pain, arthralgia, haematuria ± proteinuria (mesangial IgA on biopsy)

cards.front: Anti-GBM disease: target antigen and treatment?
cards.back: **α3 chain of type IV collagen**; treat with **plasma exchange + steroids + cyclophosphamide**

cards.front: Spot PCR equivalent to nephrotic-range proteinuria (Davidson)?
Three immunofluorescence patterns in RPGN and their causes?
cards.back: **Linear** = anti-GBM; **granular** = immune complex (post-infectious, SLE, IgA/HSP, cryo, MCGN); **negative** = pauci-immune ANCA vasculitis

cards.front: Membranous nephropathy: silver-stain and EM appearance?
cards.back: GBM **'spikes'** on silver stain; **subepithelial** electron-dense deposits between them; granular IgG on IF
Lesion in **> 50%** of glomeruli (focal = some; segmental = part of one glomerulus)
Urinary loss of **antithrombin III, protein C and S** + increased hepatic procoagulant synthesis

cards.front: Commonest causes of AKI in a nephrotic patient?
cards.back: **Hypovolaemia** (often after diuretics) or **renal vein thrombosis**, not usually progression of the GN

cards.front: Causes of GN with low serum complement (Davidson)?
cards.back: Post-infectious GN, endocarditis/subacute infection, SLE, cryoglobulinaemia, MCGN (usually complement type)

cards.front: GN with a visceral abscess: complement and biopsy?
cards.back: Complement **normal**; **no immune deposits**; mimics post-infectious GN

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had 3 weeks of swollen ankles and puffy eyes in the mornings, and her urine looks foamy. BP is 124/78 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. Spot protein:creatinine ratio is 520 mg/mmol, serum albumin 19 g/L and total cholesterol 9.1 mmol/L. Creatinine is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which clinical syndrome best describes her presentation?
questions.explanation: PCR > 350 mg/mmol is nephrotic-range proteinuria (≈ > 3.5 g/24 h). With low albumin and oedema, this meets the definition of nephrotic syndrome; high cholesterol is the usual accompaniment. There is no haematuria, hypertension or renal impairment, so the picture is not nephritic.
whyNot: Nephritic syndrome needs haematuria with hypertension, oliguria and falling GFR; she has none of these.
RPGN means renal function lost over days to weeks; her creatinine is normal.
She is symptomatic with oedema and low albumin, so this is not an isolated urinary finding.
Orthostatic proteinuria is under 1 g/day, benign and does not cause oedema or hypoalbuminaemia.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has pitting oedema up to the thighs and scrotal swelling. Serum albumin is 21 g/L. He has no history of heart or liver disease. You are deciding whether the oedema is renal or cardiac in origin.
questions.leadIn: Which examination finding most supports nephrotic syndrome rather than cardiac failure?
questions.explanation: The JVP is not raised in nephrotic oedema (it is normal or even low) except when oliguric renal failure coexists. A raised JVP points to heart failure. The other findings occur in any cause of generalised oedema and do not discriminate.
whyNot: Dependent ankle oedema occurs in both cardiac and nephrotic oedema.
Sacral oedema simply reflects posture in bed and occurs in both.
Pleural effusions are common in nephrotic syndrome but also in heart failure.
Ascites occurs in nephrotic syndrome but also in heart failure and especially in liver disease, so it does not discriminate.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most likely diagnosis in the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy develops puffy eyelids and then swollen legs a week after a cold. Urine has heavy protein and no blood; BP and creatinine are normal. Protein electrophoresis of the urine shows albumin but almost no immunoglobulin.
items.explanation: Young boy, abrupt nephrotic syndrome, no haematuria or hypertension, and highly selective proteinuria: minimal change disease, which causes about 90% of childhood nephrotic syndrome. Treat with steroids without biopsy.

items.stem: A 57-year-old white man has had slowly worsening leg oedema for 4 months. He is not diabetic, takes no regular drugs and cancer screening is negative. Serum anti-PLA2R antibody is strongly positive.
items.explanation: Indolent nephrotic syndrome in a middle-aged Caucasian man with anti-PLA2R antibodies: idiopathic (autoimmune) membranous nephropathy, the commonest adult cause in this group.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man whose parents are from Ghana presents with sudden severe nephrotic syndrome, microscopic haematuria and BP 158/96 mmHg. HIV test is negative. After 4 months of high-dose prednisolone he is still nephrotic. Biopsy shows scars in parts of some glomeruli, with IgM and C3 in the scars.
items.explanation: Two steps: a poor response to months of steroids plus segmental scars in some glomeruli means FSGS; a negative HIV test and no other secondary cause make it primary FSGS, which is common in people of West African descent (APOL1).

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most likely diagnosis in the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 21-year-old student notices red urine 1 day after developing a sore throat. He had a similar episode last winter. BP is 146/92 mmHg. Serum C3 is normal.
items.explanation: Visible haematuria within a day or two of a URTI, recurrent, with hypertension and normal complement: IgA nephropathy. PSGN would come weeks later with low C3.

items.stem: An 8-year-old girl has dark brown urine, puffy eyes and BP 140/95 mmHg. She had tonsillitis about 10 days earlier, which has settled. ASO titre is raised and C3 is low.
items.explanation: Nephritic syndrome about 10 days after streptococcal throat infection, raised ASOT and low C3: post-streptococcal GN. Treatment is supportive.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man has coughed up blood for a week and now passes little urine. Creatinine has risen from normal to 540 µmol/L over 2 weeks. ANCA is negative. Biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli with a continuous ribbon of IgG along the capillary walls.
items.explanation: Lung haemorrhage plus RPGN with linear IgG along the GBM: anti-GBM (Goodpasture's) disease, typical of younger patients. Negative ANCA and the linear pattern exclude GPA, which is pauci-immune.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has lost weight and his creatinine has risen from 95 to 410 µmol/L over 3 weeks. Urine shows red cell casts. Renal biopsy shows segmental necrosis and crescents; immunofluorescence shows little or no immunoglobulin or complement.
questions.leadIn: Which serum test is most likely to be positive?
questions.explanation: RPGN with focal necrotising, crescentic GN and negative ('pauci-immune') immunofluorescence is the pattern of small-vessel vasculitis, usually ANCA-associated. Linear IF would suggest anti-GBM; granular IF suggests immune-complex disease.
whyNot: Anti-GBM disease gives linear IgG along the GBM, not negative IF.
Post-streptococcal GN is immune-complex disease with granular deposits.
Lupus nephritis gives a granular 'full house' IF pattern.
Anti-PLA2R marks membranous nephropathy, a nephrotic, non-crescentic disease.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old army recruit has protein 1+ and no blood on dipstick at his medical. He is well, BP is 118/70 mmHg and creatinine is normal. A first-morning urine sample is negative for protein, but a sample taken later the same day is positive. Measured protein excretion is 0.4 g/24 h.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Proteinuria under 1 g/day that appears only when upright, with a negative early-morning sample, is orthostatic proteinuria: a benign condition needing no treatment. This is why proteinuria should be tested on an early-morning sample.
whyNot: IgA nephropathy causes haematuria (usually non-visible) and often hypertension; this urine has no blood.
Minimal change causes heavy, persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria with oedema.
Tubular proteinuria reflects tubular damage and would not disappear from the early-morning sample.
He has no history of diabetes, and proteinuria that is present only when upright fits the orthostatic pattern instead.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with membranous nephropathy and serum albumin 17 g/L suddenly develops left loin pain and visible haematuria. His creatinine rises from 110 to 190 µmol/L. Doppler ultrasound shows a clot in the left renal vein.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains his predisposition to this complication?
options: Urinary loss of antithrombin III and proteins C and S
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome is prothrombotic because natural anticoagulants (antithrombin III, proteins C and S) are lost in the urine while the liver makes more procoagulant factors. Renal vein thrombosis is especially common in membranous nephropathy and needs long-term anticoagulation.
whyNot: Immunoglobulin loss explains infection risk, not thrombosis.
Raised lipoprotein synthesis causes hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis, not acute venous clots.
Secondary hyperaldosteronism contributes to sodium retention and oedema.
Low oncotic pressure contributes to oedema, not to clotting.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome from minimal change disease has been given high-dose furosemide plus metolazone for a week. Her oedema has largely gone, but she is dizzy on standing (BP lying 108/66, standing 86/54 mmHg) and her creatinine has risen from 80 to 165 µmol/L. Urine output has fallen. Ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys with patent renal veins.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of her acute kidney injury?
questions.explanation: AKI in nephrotic syndrome is rarely due to the glomerular disease itself. After aggressive diuresis, postural hypotension and a rising creatinine point to hypovolaemia. Minimal change also does not usually progress to CKD.
whyNot: Minimal change disease typically does not progress, and the timing fits the diuretics.
The renal veins are patent on ultrasound.
There is nothing to suggest a nephritic process (no active sediment or hypertension), and minimal change is non-inflammatory.
Ultrasound would show hydronephrosis; it was normal.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most likely diagnosis in the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 49-year-old former intravenous drug user has a purpuric rash on both legs, joint pains and swollen ankles. Urine shows blood and 3 g/day protein. C3 is low and hepatitis C RNA is positive. A blood sample left in the cold forms a precipitate.
items.explanation: Hepatitis C, palpable purpura, arthralgia, mixed nephritic–nephrotic picture, low complement and cold-precipitating proteins: cryoglobulinaemic GN (type II). Treat the HCV with direct-acting antivirals.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has mouth ulcers, painful hands and ankle oedema. Urine shows blood and heavy protein. C3, C4 and C1q are all low. Biopsy IF stains for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C4 and C1q.
items.explanation: Young woman with systemic features, low C3, C4 and especially C1q, and 'full house' immunofluorescence: lupus nephritis.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man is treated for a lung abscess. During the illness he develops haematuria, hypertension and a rising creatinine. Serum C3 and C4 are normal, and renal biopsy shows proliferative GN with no immune deposits.
items.explanation: Two steps: a nephritic picture during infection suggests infection-related GN, but normal complement and absent immune deposits are the clues to GN with a visceral (usually pulmonary) abscess rather than post-infectious or endocarditis GN, which consume complement.

questions.theme: Renal biopsy findings in glomerular disease
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the biopsy finding you would most expect to see. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Normal light microscopy with foot-process fusion on EM
Thickened GBM with spikes and granular subepithelial IgG
Diffuse endocapillary proliferation with neutrophils and 'lumpy-bumpy' granular deposits
Ribbon-like intramembranous dense deposits staining for C3 only
Congo red-positive deposits with apple-green birefringence
'Full house' immunofluorescence (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q)

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with back pain, anaemia and a serum paraprotein has nephrotic syndrome. Ultrasound shows both kidneys are large.
items.explanation: Paraprotein plus nephrotic syndrome and enlarged kidneys suggests AL amyloid. Deposits stain with Congo red and give apple-green birefringence.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with photosensitive rash and positive anti-dsDNA has haematuria, proteinuria and low C3, C4 and C1q.
items.explanation: Lupus nephritis classically stains for all immunoglobulins and complement components including C1q: the 'full house' pattern.

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl has lost fat from her face and upper body. She has haematuria and proteinuria, persistently low C3, and C3 nephritic factor is detected.
items.explanation: Partial lipodystrophy, C3 nephritic factor and low C3 point to the complement type of MCGN, dense deposit disease, with intramembranous C3-only deposits.

items.stem: A 66-year-old heavy smoker with weight loss develops nephrotic syndrome. Anti-PLA2R antibody is negative; anti-THSD7A is positive. Chest X-ray shows a hilar mass.
items.explanation: Two steps: anti-THSD7A in a PLA2R-negative patient is linked to underlying cancer, and carcinoma (e.g. lung) causes secondary membranous nephropathy, whose biopsy shows thick GBM, spikes and granular subepithelial IgG.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old white woman, not diabetic, has developed leg oedema gradually over 5 months. Urine PCR is 610 mg/mmol with no haematuria, serum albumin 22 g/L and creatinine normal. Hepatitis serology, ANA and HIV are negative.
questions.leadIn: Which glomerular lesion is most likely on biopsy?
questions.explanation: Davidson names membranous nephropathy as the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in Caucasian adults. Its onset is indolent, in middle-aged to older patients, with a bland sediment. The negative secondary-cause screen fits idiopathic disease.
whyNot: Minimal change accounts for only about a quarter of adult cases and usually starts abruptly.
Some quick sources call FSGS the commonest adult cause, but Davidson favours membranous in Caucasian adults; FSGS is typical in people of West African descent.
IgA nephropathy presents with haematuria, not bland nephrotic syndrome.
MCGN usually gives haematuria and an active sediment with low complement.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has haemoptysis and a creatinine of 380 µmol/L that has doubled in a week. He still passes urine. Serum anti-GBM antibody is strongly positive and biopsy shows linear IgG with crescents.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Plasma exchange with glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide
ACE inhibitor and loop diuretic only
questions.explanation: Anti-GBM disease is treated with plasma exchange to remove circulating antibody, steroids to damp inflammation and cyclophosphamide to stop new antibody production. Start urgently: once oliguric or dialysis-dependent, renal function rarely recovers.
whyNot: Steroids alone do not remove circulating antibody or stop its production.
This is autoimmune, not infective.
Supportive treatment alone will not halt crescentic anti-GBM disease.
Antivirals treat hepatitis C cryoglobulinaemia, not anti-GBM disease.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man started a new tablet for knee osteoarthritis 4 weeks ago. He now has sudden heavy proteinuria (PCR 900 mg/mmol), albumin 18 g/L and oedema, without haematuria. Biopsy shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy and foot-process fusion on EM.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: The biopsy shows minimal change disease, and NSAIDs are the commonest drug cause. NSAIDs can also cause membranous nephropathy, so always take a drug history in nephrotic syndrome.
whyNot: Paracetamol is not a recognised cause of minimal change disease.
Amlodipine causes ankle oedema but not proteinuria.
Statins are used to treat nephrotic hyperlipidaemia; they are not a cause.
Metformin is not linked to minimal change disease and is not an arthritis drug.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with relapsing nephrotic syndrome develops fever, diffuse abdominal pain and a tense, tender abdomen. Ascitic fluid shows many neutrophils and Gram-positive diplococci.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Urinary loss of immunoglobulins makes nephrotic patients prone to encapsulated bacteria, especially pneumococcus (and meningococcus). Pneumococcal sepsis is a major cause of death, so pneumococcal vaccination is advised.
whyNot: E. coli is a Gram-negative rod, not a Gram-positive diplococcus.
Pneumocystis is an opportunistic fungus that causes pneumonia, not peritonitis, and is not Gram-positive diplococci.
Candida is a yeast and would not appear as Gram-positive diplococci.
TB peritonitis is chronic and lymphocytic, without diplococci on Gram stain.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presents with cola-coloured urine and swollen eyelids. Three weeks ago he had infected sores on his legs. BP is 138/92 mmHg, creatinine is mildly raised, urine shows red cell casts, C3 is low and anti-streptococcal antibodies are raised. He is passing reasonable volumes of urine.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Supportive care with salt restriction, diuretics and blood pressure control
Urgent renal biopsy before any treatment
questions.explanation: Step 1: nephritic syndrome (haematuria with casts, hypertension, oedema). Step 2: it follows a skin infection by weeks, with low C3 and streptococcal serology, so it is post-streptococcal GN (latency is longer after skin than throat infection). Step 3: PSGN is self-limiting, so treat supportively with salt and fluid restriction, diuretics and antihypertensives, and dialysis only if needed. Antibiotics are rarely needed because the infection has gone, and a clear-cut case does not need a biopsy. Children usually recover fully.
whyNot: Steroids are not first-line: PSGN usually resolves on its own, and they are considered only if recovery is slow or disease is severe.
Plasma exchange is for anti-GBM disease.
Cyclophosphamide is for ANCA vasculitis, anti-GBM disease or severe lupus.
Biopsy is usually unnecessary when the picture is clearly post-streptococcal.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man has severe nephrotic syndrome. His first biopsy contained 6 glomeruli, all normal on light microscopy, with foot-process fusion on EM. He was treated as minimal change disease but is still nephrotic after 16 weeks of high-dose prednisolone. A repeat biopsy with 25 glomeruli shows scarring in parts of several glomeruli.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Step 1: FSGS is focal, so a small sample can miss the scarred glomeruli and look like minimal change. Step 2: poor response to steroids is a clue, since primary FSGS responds less often and less fully than minimal change. Step 3: the larger biopsy shows segmental sclerosis, which confirms FSGS. Remember that primary FSGS may need up to 6 months of steroids before being called resistant, and it often recurs after transplantation.
whyNot: The repeat biopsy shows segmental scars, which minimal change does not produce.
Membranous would show a thick GBM with granular subepithelial IgG.
IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA and presents with haematuria.
Amyloid deposits would be seen on light microscopy and stain with Congo red.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman has persistent non-visible haematuria and BP 150/95 mmHg. Spot urine protein:creatinine ratio is 180 mg/mmol. eGFR is 70 mL/min/1.73 m².
questions.leadIn: How is her proteinuria best interpreted?
options: About 1–3.5 g/24 h, so glomerular disease is likely
questions.explanation: Step 1: a PCR of 100–350 mg/mmol equals roughly 1–3.5 g/24 h; nephrotic range starts above 350. Step 2: over 1 g/day makes glomerular disease likely, and combined with haematuria and hypertension this needs nephrology referral. Step 3: adult glomerular proteinuria (PCR > 100) is an indication to consider renal biopsy.
whyNot: Nephrotic range is PCR > 350 mg/mmol.
Normal PCR is under 25 mg/mmol.
Tubular proteinuria tops out at a PCR of about 150–200 mg/mmol, so size alone does not exclude it, but persistent haematuria with hypertension points to the glomerulus.
Orthostatic proteinuria is under 1 g/day and occurs in otherwise well people without haematuria or hypertension.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most useful next investigation in the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: ASO titre with C3 and C4
Serum free light chains and protein electrophoresis
Repeat protein test on an early-morning urine sample
Renal ultrasound for size before biopsy

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has persistent microscopic haematuria and mild proteinuria. His maternal uncle started dialysis at 35, and he finds it hard to hear high-pitched sounds.
items.explanation: Haematuria, family history on the maternal side (X-linked) and high-frequency hearing loss suggest Alport syndrome: check with genetic screening and a hearing test.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has months of nasal crusting and sinusitis, then haemoptysis and creatinine rising over 2 weeks. Urine shows red cell casts.
items.explanation: Upper airway disease, lung involvement and RPGN suggest granulomatosis with polyangiitis: check ANCA (PR3-ANCA is positive in > 90% of active GPA).

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has back pain, normocytic anaemia, hypercalcaemia and new nephrotic-range proteinuria.
items.explanation: Two steps: back pain, anaemia and hypercalcaemia suggest myeloma; nephrotic proteinuria then suggests AL amyloid. Check immunoglobulins, protein electrophoresis, Bence Jones protein and serum free light chains.

items.stem: A fit 17-year-old has 1+ protein on a dipstick done in the afternoon at a sports medical. BP, creatinine and urine microscopy are normal.
items.explanation: Low-grade proteinuria in a well adolescent may be orthostatic. Repeat on a first-morning sample; if negative, it is benign.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most appropriate main treatment in the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Oral prednisolone about 1 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks
Plasma exchange with glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide
Glucocorticoids with IV cyclophosphamide or rituximab
Supportive care only: salt restriction, diuretics, BP control
ACE inhibitor or ARB as the main therapy
Rituximab, or an alkylating agent with steroids
Antiretroviral therapy with an ACE inhibitor

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy has typical nephrotic syndrome with no haematuria, normal BP and normal creatinine.
items.explanation: Childhood nephrotic syndrome is almost always minimal change: treat with high-dose prednisolone without biopsy, and biopsy only if it fails.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy has BP 150/94 mmHg, proteinuria 1.2 g/day and stable eGFR.
items.explanation: IgA nephropathy is managed mainly by BP control, preferring RAS blockade when there is proteinuria. There is no strong evidence for routine immunosuppression.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has nephritic–nephrotic syndrome, purpura and low complement. Cryoglobulins are present and hepatitis C RNA is positive.
items.explanation: HCV-related cryoglobulinaemic GN: treat the cause with direct-acting antivirals.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with anti-PLA2R-positive membranous nephropathy remains heavily nephrotic after 6 months of ACE inhibitor, diuretic and statin, and his eGFR is falling.
items.explanation: Severe or progressive idiopathic membranous needs immunosuppression: rituximab, or an alkylating agent (cyclophosphamide/chlorambucil) with steroids. Steroids alone do not work.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman develops fever, arthralgia, haemoptysis and a rapidly rising creatinine. Urine shows red cell casts and high-titre MPO-ANCA is positive. Her regular medicines are hydralazine, amlodipine, bendroflumethiazide, atorvastatin and aspirin, all taken for several years.
questions.leadIn: Which of her medicines is most likely to have triggered this illness?
questions.explanation: Hydralazine is a classic cause of drug-induced ANCA vasculitis, usually with high-titre MPO-ANCA. Others include propylthiouracil, minocycline and penicillamine.
whyNot: Amlodipine is not a recognised cause of ANCA vasculitis.
Thiazides are not linked to ANCA-associated GN.
Statins are not a recognised trigger of ANCA vasculitis.
Aspirin is not a recognised trigger of ANCA vasculitis.

questions.stem: Several patients with biopsy-proven glomerulonephritis are being assessed to decide who most needs immunosuppressive therapy.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is a recognised poor prognostic indicator in glomerular disease?
questions.explanation: Davidson lists male sex, hypertension, persistent heavy proteinuria, raised creatinine at presentation, rapid decline in function and tubulo-interstitial fibrosis on biopsy as poor prognostic signs common to all GN.
whyNot: Male sex, not female sex, is the adverse factor.
A raised creatinine at presentation is adverse; a normal one is reassuring.
Persistent, severe proteinuria is adverse, not low-grade transient proteinuria.
Hypertension, not normotension, predicts a worse course.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the most likely explanation in the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Gut-wall oedema reducing oral diuretic absorption

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with membranous nephropathy develops sudden right loin pain, visible haematuria and a 40% rise in creatinine. He is euvolaemic and has not changed his medicines.
items.explanation: Loin pain, haematuria and falling function in a membranous patient: renal vein thrombosis, from loss of antithrombin III and proteins C/S. Look on ultrasound and anticoagulate long term.

items.stem: A 5-year-old girl with relapsing nephrotic syndrome has fever, abdominal pain, rebound tenderness and tense ascites.
items.explanation: Immunoglobulin loss predisposes to encapsulated bacteria: spontaneous pneumococcal peritonitis in a child with nephrotic ascites. Pneumococcal sepsis is a major cause of death.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with gross oedema gets no diuresis from oral furosemide 120 mg daily, despite good adherence and a salt-restricted diet. The same dose given intravenously produces a brisk diuresis.
items.explanation: Two steps: failure orally but success IV means the drug was not reaching the circulation; in nephrotic syndrome, oedema of the gut wall impairs absorption, so IV diuretics may be needed.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman's creatinine rises from 88 to 430 µmol/L over 3 weeks. She is hypertensive and oedematous. Urine shows blood, red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is most likely on renal biopsy?
options: Crescents of inflammatory cells in Bowman's space
Normal glomeruli with foot-process fusion only
questions.explanation: Loss of renal function over days to weeks with an active sediment is rapidly progressive GN, whose typical biopsy lesion is crescent formation (often with necrosis in vasculitis).
whyNot: Foot-process fusion alone is minimal change, which is nephrotic without an active sediment.
Spikes and subepithelial deposits mean membranous nephropathy, an indolent nephrotic disease.
Segmental sclerosis is FSGS, mainly a nephrotic disease.
Amyloid causes nephrotic syndrome and large kidneys, not an active sediment with RPGN.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man has haematuria, proteinuria of 2.5 g/day and mild hypertension. Serum C3 is persistently low on three samples over 4 months. ASO titre, ANA and ANCA are negative.
questions.leadIn: Which glomerular disease is most likely?
questions.explanation: Persistently low C3 with a mixed nephritic–nephrotic picture and negative tests for strep, lupus and vasculitis points to MCGN, which is on Davidson's list of low-complement GN (usually the complement type); Kumar describes persistently reduced C3 in MCGN. Post-infectious GN would follow a recent infection with a raised ASOT and is self-limiting.
whyNot: IgA nephropathy has normal complement.
Minimal change has normal complement and no haematuria.
Anti-GBM disease has normal complement and presents as RPGN.
Primary FSGS does not lower complement.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman has creatinine 820 µmol/L, is anuric and needs dialysis on admission. She has no cough or haemoptysis. Serum anti-GBM antibody is positive and biopsy shows linear IgG with crescents in almost all glomeruli.
questions.leadIn: Which feature best predicts that her kidney function will not recover?
questions.explanation: In anti-GBM disease, renal function is rarely recoverable once the patient is oliguric or needs dialysis at presentation (Kumar: creatinine above about 600–700 µmol/L). Renal-limited disease is typical in older patients, so absent lung involvement is not itself the predictor.
whyNot: Renal-limited disease is common in elderly patients and does not by itself determine renal recovery.
Age alone is not the stated predictor; the stage of renal failure at presentation is.
The antibody confirms the diagnosis but every patient has it.
Sex is not a stated predictor of renal recovery in anti-GBM disease.

ospe.identify: Immunofluorescence: granular capillary-wall IgG → membranous; mesangial IgA → IgA nephropathy; smooth linear IgG ribbon along GBM → anti-GBM (Goodpasture's)
Silver stain with GBM 'spikes' around subepithelial deposits, thick capillary walls → membranous nephropathy
Eosinophilic glomerular deposits; Congo red with apple-green birefringence under polarised light → amyloidosis
Crescent of macrophages and epithelial cells filling Bowman's space, ± segmental necrosis → rapidly progressive (crescentic) GN
Linear IF → anti-GBM disease; diffuse granular IF → immune-complex GN
'Lumpy-bumpy' (starry sky) granular IF → post-infectious GN; linear IF → Goodpasture syndrome
Double-contoured 'tramline' GBM with subendothelial deposits → type 1 MCGN; dense intramembranous ribbon → dense deposit disease
Segmental sclerosis in part of a glomerulus → FSGS; collapsed tuft with prominent podocytes → collapsing variant (HIV)
